title: Yield Storm Ahead- Preparing for a New Era - Systematic Investor 330

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/Yield Storm Ahead- Preparing for a New Era - Systematic Investor 330.docx

speakers: Jim (guest; captioned 'Jim kasang', systematic investor at Kai)
summary:
Jim and Niels (Systematic Investor series, Jan 2025): options skew, vanna/charm and opex cycles as drivers of an expected equity decline, and a structurally inflationary regime with rising yields.
Guest argues rates drive everything (P/E and margin compression as in 1968-82), equities are no inflation hedge, hedging is now harder with an upward-sloping curve, and Fed independence is at risk.
Also an asymmetric China call-option trade and a trend-following update.

coverage.note: intro; endowment group think and recency bias; 10y yield 5% call
commodity rules-based approach; populism regime change; group think
trend following update and index returns; S&P skew introduction
skew term structure, supply/demand, vanna vs gamma, CBOE SKEW index
year-end flow model, expected 10% decline and counter-trend rally, opex
stair-step decline, quarterly opex and COVID cycle, long vol
Fed timing speculation, two-year seasonal, 1968-82 analogy, election years
counter-trend rally via vanna compression; bond supply and defence spending
rates drive equities: multiples, margins, curve and hedge
equities not inflation hedge, pain trade, leveraged bond exposure, recency
hidden duration in callable bonds, private assets, inflation feedback
Fed in a box, shadow Fed, jobs/CPI importance
Fed control of vol, instability, conflict
China deal asymmetry, calls and barbell

completeness_estimate: 0.84 - the first reader captured the main thesis chain (skew and opex flows, 1968-82 analogy, rates-drive-everything, hidden duration, Fed independence, China asymmetry) and the numbers well; it missed several secondary points (back-end skew persistence, jobs-data reaction at 5% yields, near-term S&P view, hedge sizing, long-end decoupling risk, rate-cycle length, the 1990 look-back example, institutional failure, the China-deal counter-argument).

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: how much group think uh there was how uh not open to uh the possibility that the 60 or the 4 might not work
claims.claim: Endowment professionals are crowding into private equity and venture (65/35 type allocations) and are unwilling to consider that 60/40 may fail, which the guest reads as recency bias.
claims.conditions: after a long period of falling rates

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: yields spiking 5% which we thought would be by December 31st we called that we were about 10 days late here
claims.claim: The guest's call that the 10-year yield would reach 5% (and 6.5% this year) was roughly on track, and he expects higher yields to have massive effects this year.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: something you cannot really participate in unless you have uh a very um sort of rules based uh approach because they're hard to forecast
claims.claim: Commodity prices are driven by hard-to-forecast natural events (weather, fires), so they can only be traded with a rules-based approach.
claims.testable: partly: argument for systematic trend rules

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: Trump is a vehicle for something much bigger than than who Trump is in my opinion
claims.claim: Populist, protectionist sentiment is a structural trend that Trump accelerates, and the guest sees a regime change comparable to earlier periods, with the 10-year Treasury signalling it.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: group thinking and recency bias and all of that maybe those are the two worst things you could be exposed to right now
claims.claim: Group-think and recency bias are the largest risks when the world may change dramatically over the next four years.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: long equities long US dollar seems to be very constructive for Trend followers at the moment
claims.claim: Early 2025 trends in long equities, long US dollar, live cattle, gold, silver and grains are generous to trend followers while UK and French yields hit highs.
claims.direction: long equities, long USD, long gold/silver/grains/cattle

correction.issue: Overstates France: the speaker says the UK is hitting very high yield levels ('a bond crisis') and France is 'having some challenges'; he does not say French yields hit highs.
correction.fix: Early 2025 trends in long equities, long US dollar, live cattle, gold, silver and grains are generous to trend followers, while UK yields are at very high levels (a bond crisis) and France is also facing bond-market challenges.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own Trend barometer is strong at the moment it's close at 59 yesterday so that should indicate a good start to 2025 for Trend followers
claims.claim: A strong trend barometer reading (59) indicates a good start for trend followers.
claims.testable: yes: barometer vs forward trend index returns

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: index for 20e maturity or more uh and this is before today's uh events down 1.88%
claims.claim: Long-dated (20+ year) Treasuries were down 1.88% YTD, versus CTA indices up 85 bp, S&P 500 up 62 bp, a data point on bond weakness helping trend followers.
claims.indicator: S&P US Treasury Bond 20+ year index

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: once you get out to two three four months that skew uh has has continued to be very sticky and steep
claims.claim: Long-dated (2-4 month) S&P 500 index skew (downside put volatility relative to upside) remains sticky and steep, which the guest treats as a systematic warning indicator.
claims.conditions: after the August 2024 meltdown and election

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: all of that skew uh demand is played a huge driver which we discussed here in that August decline
claims.claim: Structured product demand, quarterly options expiration open interest and event hedging (election, December opex) drive demand for long-dated skew.
claims.indicator: structured product and options open interest
claims.testable: partly: flows hard to observe directly

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: we had a historic breakdown between short-term and long-term skew invol
claims.claim: August 2024 produced a historic breakdown between short-term and long-term skew after a fast, large move when front-of-curve skew supply was ample.
claims.indicator: short vs long dated skew spread

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: there is a structural supply and demand imbalance um on the downside options further out out and and the curve and that can that can lead to um again a reinforcing down structural down move
claims.claim: A supply/demand imbalance in long-dated downside options, where dealers short skew must sell more far skew to cover, can reinforce and lengthen a decline (analogs 1998-99, 2007-08, LTCM mark-to-market), though not a short-term spike since short-dated skew is well supplied.
claims.conditions: skew stays bid in back end of curve
claims.testable: partly: skew vs forward drawdown testable but few episodes

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: we continue to see more Vaga response relative to to um you know gamma in the market
claims.claim: Vanna (vol-driven) dealer hedging flows dominate gamma in the market, which can turn a vol event into a multi-year decline.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: it is not a good measure of skew um uh and and the best measure for skew without getting too wonky is a Delta sticky um measure something that's probabilistic as opposed to Mone based
claims.claim: The CBOE SKEW index is a poor measure of skew; a delta-based (probabilistic) measure is better than a moneyness-based one.
claims.indicator: CBOE SKEW index vs delta-sticky skew

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: both V and charm flows that we talk about the rebalancing Rel leveraging effect at the end of the year
claims.claim: The guest's calendar-flow model (vanna and charm flows, year-end rebalancing and re-leveraging) pointed to the year-end rally ending early before the late-December decline.
claims.testable: partly: dealer flow models not public

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: there will be a counter Trend rally and that counter Trend rally will be to will be sold
claims.claim: Guest expects a roughly 10% peak-to-trough decline as the beginning of a bigger decline, with a counter-trend rally that will be sold.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: Opex Fridays and the Mondays are usually the strongest day and 95% of time but when they're not they're incredibly
claims.claim: Opex Fridays and following Mondays are usually strong (about 95% of the time) but when they are not the move is violent due to large open interest.
claims.conditions: large open interest in January monthly opex

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: the most painful trade which is the most likely trade is uh you know if that's well supplied and the longterm skew is bid is for a stair step down
claims.claim: With short-dated skew well supplied and long-dated skew bid, the expected path is a stair-step decline, as short-dated puts fail to protect and hedgers are forced to buy long-dated skew.
claims.conditions: well supplied front skew and bid back skew

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: quarterly expirations are the biggest risk um the structural product issuance is bigger than ever positioning is bigger than ever
claims.claim: Quarterly expirations are the biggest risk, with record structured product issuance and positioning, making March opex a real risk.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: we knew about Co we rallied till F the day after FB Opex and then um you know sharp decline
claims.claim: The COVID crash ran from the day after Feb opex to the day after March opex (about 30% option-cycle to option-cycle), an example of options and structured products accelerating declines; a similar Feb-to-March cycle is flagged.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: ball is is actually uh was really cheap in December and was likely to Rally into uh throughout q1
claims.claim: Long-term volatility was cheap in December and likely to rally through Q1, which is how the guest plans to play the view.
claims.testable: yes: vol level vs forward return

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: knowledge is all dampening if I go out there start talking about it too much it becomes increasingly unlikely
claims.claim: Widely publicised flow patterns become less likely to occur as participants front-run them.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: maybe the FED is fully aware of these cycles and that's why they waited until the 23rd of March to come out and do all of that stuff
claims.claim: Speculation that the Fed times interventions to after March opex, aware of options expiration risk cycles.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: two years back to back positive like that uh has an expected negative return the following year which you don't see in many data sets
claims.claim: After the S&P 500's best two-year calendar run since 1988, back-to-back strong years have historically meant negative expected return and poor win rate in the next year.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: 68 to 82 incredibly uh poor Equity performance 67% real uh negative returns over 14 years
claims.claim: In the last structurally inflationary period (1968-82) equities lost about 67% in real terms over 14 years; populism and protection are seen as recreating that regime.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: during election years the average performance was 21% uh over that same period so the non-election years during that cycle are pitiful
claims.claim: In 1968-82 equity gains were concentrated in election years (average 21%) while non-election years were poor, so strong election-year returns are in line with history.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: all of the populist elections all five if you include the last two uh have a very similar they 100% uh up double digits the average return 22%
claims.claim: All five populist-era elections saw double-digit equity gains (average 22%) versus about 5% for other elections, which the guest sees as an outlier that will be given back.
claims.indicator: equity return in populist election years

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: I really think there's some give back here for lack of a better term uh given what I would say is bringing forward uh you know uh Equity Market performance
claims.claim: Election-year spending and market boosts bring performance forward and are likely to be given back after the election.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: the V which is now expanded now compresses and that compression much like we saw in August sharp feet bottom
claims.claim: If a decline slows, expanded vanna compresses and the reversal produces a sharp counter-trend rally (as in August and COVID), with January opex the biggest for single stocks.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you have record issuing of corporate bonds uh they're estimated of being at around $200 billion doar in in January
claims.claim: Record corporate bond issuance (about $200bn in January per Bloomberg) and possibly fewer bond buyers add to supply pressure on yields.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Trump saying that actually NATO countries should probably spend 5% of their GDP on Military
claims.claim: NATO defence spending of 5% of GDP would mean larger deficits and more government bond issuance.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: performance of equity markets and and assets at large can be very poor uh throughout a very strong economy
claims.claim: Rising interest rates, not economic strength, drive asset returns: in 1968-82 GDP grew above trend yet equities returned zero nominal and fell 67% real.
claims.direction: equities down when rates rise secularly
claims.testable: yes: rate regime vs real returns

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: if you can get a a 20% yield on a 10year bond you're not going to pay a 25 PE for for the market multiple contractions
claims.claim: Higher bond yields compress equity P/E multiples (25x in 1968 to about 4.5x in 1982, a 20% earnings yield).
claims.testable: yes: earnings yield vs bond yield

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: the second biggest one is margin contraction we are sitting at record margins
claims.claim: Margin contraction is the second driver: margins are at record levels and would fall if rates stay higher for a secular period.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: if if the curve is inverted you're getting paid to to hedge uh your interest rate inflation risk
claims.claim: An inverted yield curve paid investors to hedge rate and inflation risk; with the curve upward sloping, the hedge is now harder and costlier.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: were suggesting equities as a hedge to um to inflation uh that is a a complete misunderstanding of of what equities do during structural structural inflationary periods
claims.claim: Equities are not an inflation hedge during structural inflationary periods, despite what most seasoned professionals say.
claims.testable: yes: real equity returns by inflation regime

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: the pain trades generally work because that means people are stuck that's a sequestered demand or Supply that needs to come back to the market
claims.claim: Pain trades usually work (over 90%) because stuck participants must eventually trade, so the trend in yields will continue and accelerate when they are stopped out.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: and there are enough B enties that are leveraged with Bond exposure uh and all kinds of way across the market it's just too much exposure relative to what the market can handle
claims.claim: Leveraged long-bond exposures across the market and heavy issuance (e.g. Europe) are too large for market capacity, so bond vigilantes can push yields higher.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: most of the portfolio managers out there have never experienced an interest rate increase or hiking
claims.claim: Most portfolio managers have never lived through a rate-hiking cycle, so recency bias leaves them unprepared for structurally rising rates.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: the call essentially means if yields go up right um you know one or two% all of a sudden the call comes off the table it's that it's just premium that you've collected now your effective duration goes to 15
claims.claim: Callable municipal bonds hide duration risk: if yields rise 1-2% the call is no longer exercised and effective duration jumps from about 5 to 15 years.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: it's not just duration risk it's liquidity risk
claims.claim: Private equity, private credit and other private assets carry both duration and liquidity risk when rates rise.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: the cost of money is a driver itself to inflation
claims.claim: Higher interest rates feed back into inflation through the cost of goods, so rising rates are partly self-reinforcing.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: the more inflation expectations go higher the more people pull forward demand try and buy inventory try and lock up Goods
claims.claim: In the 1960s-70s rising inflation expectations led people to pull forward demand and buy inventory, making inflation nonlinear and self-reinforcing.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: they could push use their tools to help uh counteract inflation while spurring demand and and now that they're contradictory
claims.claim: The Fed dominated outcomes when deflation was structural, but with inflation and growth objectives now in conflict it is in a box.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: I 100% expect him to put in a quote unquote Shadow fed
claims.claim: Guest expects Trump to name a shadow Fed chair early to pressure Powell, citing a Nixon analogy, so Fed independence is a risk.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: so this is a much bigger uh number today as will the CPI number be than we've seen a long time
claims.claim: The January jobs and CPI releases are unusually important given Fed uncertainty and narrative control.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: the Federal Reserve has the ability to linearly control volatility that that drives and drive and drive money to corporations
claims.claim: Under a fiat reserve currency the Fed's ability to control volatility drove money to corporations and supported globalization and the long period of peace and stability.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: there's more realized vol come because there's less stability
claims.claim: As the Fed loses its dominant role, more realized volatility and geopolitical conflict follow as institutions and countries pull levers of power.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: just uh expect more global conflict
claims.claim: Expect more global conflict and breakdown of institutions because power is being questioned.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: we're seeing a a you know 50y year uh type dislocation relative to assets
claims.claim: Chinese assets are abandoned while US assets and the dollar are extremely favoured, a roughly 50-year dislocation whose reversion needs a catalyst.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: can Trump who is very very pro- Russia for lack of a better term be super uh strong against China
claims.claim: Trump may be less hard on China than expected because of Russia-China alignment and statements on Taiwan cost, and tariffs may target Canada and Mexico instead.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: it took a Nixon to open up China
claims.claim: Trump could do a deal with China (Nixon analog), which would be short-term supportive and reduce inflation pressure.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: it's about probability times magnitude I'm saying some people I think think this is a 2% chance I'm saying it's a 30 40% chance
claims.claim: A China reversion is an asymmetric trade: guest estimates a 30-40% chance versus the market's roughly 2%, with a very large payoff.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: go buy calls and get asymmetric convexity barbell
claims.claim: Express it with calls in a barbell alongside inflation-oriented positioning, rather than all-in Chinese stocks.
claims.direction: long China calls plus inflation hedges

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: elon's incentives are also different than Trump's and may help push Trump's you know incentives in a certain direction
claims.claim: Musk's incentives may push the administration towards a short-term China deal, while narrative shifts move outcomes.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: but that will create more volatility uh and more dispersion and more of the issues um you know uh rotations that we've been seeing
claims.claim: Narrative-driven political influence will produce more volatility, dispersion and rotations in markets.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: they're in a bit of a bond crisis for sure France also having some challenges
claims.claim: UK gilt yields have reached very high levels (a 'bond crisis') and France is also struggling, so long-end sovereign bond stress is spreading beyond the US, which supports the guest's higher-yield thesis and helps short-bond trend positions.
claims.indicator: UK gilt and French government bond yields
claims.testable: yes - gilt and OAT yield series

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: soen Trend doing a little bit worse uh 62 basis points as a Wednesday uh short-term Traders index is flat as a pancake uh so far this year
claims.claim: In early January 2025 the SG Trend index was up 62 bp while the SG Short-Term Traders index was flat, so longer-horizon trend exposure was paying while short-horizon CTA trading was not (data point, one week of returns).
claims.indicator: SG Trend Index vs SG Short-Term Traders Index

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: was this just a function of that end of the year Supply demand and balance and the answer is it hasn't and it hasn't in uh now it's really focused on March and April
claims.claim: Back-end skew demand did not fade after the election and the year-end structured-product rebalancing; it rolled out to March and April expiries, which shows the imbalance is structural (people are stuck short skew) and not merely a calendar effect, so it is a persisting warning sign.
claims.conditions: skew stays bid after the known event dates have passed
claims.testable: yes - skew term structure after event dates vs subsequent returns

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: we were pretty adamant that uh you know into the end of the year uh particular starting in uh late October uh should really be a constructive period
claims.claim: The guest's calendar framework treated late October into mid-January as a constructive period (best case a rally into mid-January) after a weak summer and September, with the flow model (vanna/charm, year-end rebalancing) as the check on whether the rally would end early.
claims.indicator: S&P 500 seasonal window plus vanna/charm flow estimates
claims.direction: long equities late Oct to mid-Jan unless flows are too weak
claims.conditions: fails when option-flow support is insufficient (it ended early in December 2024)
claims.testable: yes - seasonal window returns conditional on flow proxies

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: this potential decline on a strong unemployment number on a Friday very few people want to jump in front of these things
claims.claim: With the 10-year yield at 5%, a strong payrolls number is bad for equities because investors de-risk ahead of it and few will buy in front of a rates shock, so a strong jobs print can trigger the next leg down.
claims.direction: equities down on strong jobs data
claims.conditions: when the 10-year yield is at or near 5% and rate fears dominate
claims.testable: yes - equity reaction to payroll surprises conditional on yield level

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: you know 150 to 200 points in the S&P potentially uh you know uh in the next two days
claims.claim: The guest saw a possible 150-200 point S&P 500 drop within two days, agreed with the host that weakness could last to the end of Q1, and expected a re-decline because March and April skew is not well supplied (a short-term view, not a crash call).
claims.conditions: January monthly opex with large open interest
claims.testable: yes - dated forecast, checkable against S&P path in January to March 2025

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: sizing of that trade matters because I think some people put it on but as a as a trade the problem is that trade affects everything
claims.claim: The size of the rates hedge matters: a secular rise in rates damages the value of most assets, so a token position will not offset portfolio-wide losses and the hedge has to be large relative to the book.
claims.indicator: rates hedge size vs portfolio duration
claims.conditions: secular rise in long-term interest rates
claims.testable: partly - hedge sizing can be backtested, but 'large enough' is not defined

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: when things decouple which I I'm not saying they have done that yet but if they really do decouple which we saw maybe a little bit of tendency to in the UK you know things can go completely against
claims.claim: Central banks may still control the long end of the curve, but if long yields decouple from central-bank control (a small sign in the UK) yields could move sharply against holders; the host raises this as the risk to the consensus that policy can contain the long end.
claims.indicator: long-end yields vs central bank policy (UK gilts as example)
claims.conditions: decoupling of long yields from central-bank control
claims.testable: partly - gilt episode can be studied, decoupling is hard to define ex ante

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we've had 40 Years of interest rates coming down I'm not saying we're going to have 40 Years of interest rates coming up but I think they're certainly going up for for a while
claims.claim: Interest rates move in long cycles; after 40 years of falling rates the host expects a sustained rise, though not necessarily another 40 years.
claims.direction: rates up for an extended period
claims.testable: partly - long-cycle evidence is thin (few independent cycles)

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: showed a graph going back to 1990 saying that municipal bonds have never been gone above 5 and a quarter per
claims.claim: A muni manager reassured a client by showing a chart from 1990 in which muni yields never exceeded 5.25%; the sample window covers only the falling-rate era, so it understates rate-regime risk (an example of recency bias in risk assessment).
claims.conditions: risk estimated from a window that excludes the pre-1982 high-rate regime
claims.testable: yes - compare risk estimates from post-1990 vs longer samples

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: we're in a vacuum in a sense of leadership a lot of these big institutions have in many ways uh failed
claims.claim: Major global institutions (WTO after China's entry, the WHO, and the EU, whose competitiveness the Draghi report called into question) are seen as failing, leaving a leadership vacuum that adds to geopolitical and market instability.

claims.speaker: Jim
claims.quote: I have yet to see a contrary uh argument that is Meaningful except on this one issue
claims.claim: Caveat to the guest's structural-inflation, rising-yield thesis: the only meaningful counter-argument he has seen is a US-China deal and China reversion, which could ease inflation pressure and change the macro picture.
claims.direction: China deal would be disinflationary and supportive of growth
claims.conditions: if the Trump administration pursues a deal with China instead of confrontation
